title: Conjecture 1 (Scott and Seymour)
statement_text: For every positive integer $k$ there exists a $\chi$ such that, for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there is a vertex $v$ such that $\chi(G[N_{T}^{+}(v)])\geqslant k$.
context_text: Scott and Seymour conjectured this mixed graph-tournament analogue of the tournament locality result of Harutyunyan, Le, Thomassé, and Wu. The conjecture was supported by the fact that the statement holds when chromatic number is replaced by fractional chromatic number.
paper_contribution: Disproves the conjecture for all $k\geqslant 3$ by constructing $G$ and $T$ such that the out-neighbourhood of any set of at most $\frac{\log|V(T)|}{2\chi^2}$ vertices is bipartite.
notes: Attributed to [SS16] (Barbados Graph Theory Workshop 2016 open problems list); also appears as [HLTW19, Conj. 7].

title: Question 10
statement_text: Does there exist, for each integer $d$, an integer $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there is a vertex $v$ for which $G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]$ has degeneracy at least $d$?
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. For degeneracy, they show that for every $k$ there is a $k$-regular graph $G$ and a tournament $T$ on its vertex set with every $G[N^+_T(v)]$ a forest, whereas if $G$ has degeneracy at least $12k$ then some two vertices $x,y$ have $G[N^+_T(\{x,y\})]$ of degeneracy at least $k-1$. Since in their counterexamples the out-neighbourhoods induce bipartite graphs, which can still have high degeneracy, the authors have been unable to determine whether high chromatic number forces an out-neighbourhood of high degeneracy, and ask this question.

title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: For every graph $G$ with sufficiently large chromatic number, and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there exists a vertex $v$ such that $G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]$ contains a cycle.
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. For degeneracy, they show that for every $k$ there is a $k$-regular graph $G$ and a tournament $T$ on its vertex set with every $G[N^+_T(v)]$ a forest, whereas if $G$ has degeneracy at least $12k$ then some two vertices $x,y$ have $G[N^+_T(\{x,y\})]$ of degeneracy at least $k-1$. The authors ask whether, for each $d$, sufficiently large chromatic number forces some out-neighbourhood $G[N^+_T(v)]$ of degeneracy at least $d$. They suspect that this is true for $d=2$, i.e. that some out-neighbourhood must induce a subgraph containing a cycle (a graph has degeneracy at least $2$ exactly when it contains a cycle).

title: Conjecture 12
statement_text: For every positive integer $k$, there exists a $\chi$ such that if $T$ is the uniformly random tournament on vertex set $[N]$, then with high probability (as $N\to\infty$), for every graph $G$ on $[N]$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant\chi$ there is a vertex $v\in[N]$ for which $\chi(G[N^{+}_{T}(v)])\geqslant k$.
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. The tournaments in these counterexamples are very structured; the authors conjecture that, with high probability, a uniformly random tournament $T$ cannot be used instead, i.e. that the Scott–Seymour statement holds for almost every tournament.
notes: The statement as extracted likely contains a typographical omission: '$G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]\geqslant k$' should read '$\chi(G[N^{+}_{T}(v)])\geqslant k$'.

title: Conjecture 13
statement_text: There exists $f(N)$ satisfying $f(N)=o(\log N)$ such that for every $N$-vertex graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant f(N)$, and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there is a vertex $v$ for which $\chi(G[N^{+}_{T}(v)])\geqslant 3$.
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. Conversely, the bound on $|U|$ is close to optimal: $T$ has a dominating set $S$ of size at most $\lceil\log_2N\rceil$, so if $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ some collection of at most $\lceil\log_2(N)/\lfloor\chi/2-1\rfloor\rceil$ out-neighbourhoods has union inducing a subgraph of chromatic number at least $3$. The authors ask whether $o(\log(N)/\chi)$ out-neighbourhoods (as $\chi\to\infty$) suffice, and in particular conjecture that a single out-neighbourhood suffices once $\chi(G)$ exceeds some $f(N)=o(\log N)$. Note that out-neighbourhoods inducing independent sets for all $v$ force $\chi(G)\le3$.
